# Required assets

<!-- Generated by `npm run assets`. Edit src/lib/data, not this file. -->

**388 files**: 312 music files across 6 scenes, 53 ambience beds and 23 one-shots. That is 57:35 of unique music once, not per intensity. Paths assume `assetLayout({ base: "/audio", ext: "ogg" })`.

## How the music is built

A scene's score is a **pool of motifs** — short passages, chained in a shuffled order so the music runs for minutes without the sequence coming round. A motif that has just played will not be picked again for another few motifs, so the shuffle never doubles back on itself. Each motif is recorded at several **intensity levels**, which is how the arrangement thickens as a scene heats up.

So for a four-level scene, one motif is four files of the same passage:

```
intensity-1.ogg   strings
intensity-2.ogg   strings + piano
intensity-3.ogg   strings + piano + bass
intensity-4.ogg   strings + piano + bass + counter-melody
```

**Each file is a complete mix at that level**, not an additive stem. Changing intensity crossfades to that level of the *same motif at the same point in the passage*, which is why every level has to exist for every motif — there is no level 2 of motif 3 to cross to if it was never bounced. Bounce them from one session so they line up sample for sample.

The engine also supports the additive alternative — `intensityMode: "layers"`, where each file holds only its own instruments and they sum. Same file count, and the console can A/B them: `npm run dev` then the `intensity model` switch in the demo. Name additive files `layer-1.ogg` and pass `assetLayout({ musicPrefix: "layer" })`.

Exploration and combat are separate pools, not two versions of the same passage. Switching mode crossfades from one pool into the other, so combat can be its own music rather than a busier arrangement of the same cue.

## Why motifs, and not one long piece

Decoded audio is uncompressed. A 47 s stereo stem at 44.1 kHz occupies about 16 MB in memory however small the .ogg is — so a five-minute layered stem would be about 106 MB, and one scene's worth would run past a gigabyte. Long-form music cannot be held as buffers, and buffers are what make the layers line up sample for sample.

Chaining short motifs is the way out. Only the sounding motif and the one queued behind it are ever *required* to be resident, so the floor is:

```
music   47 s x 2 motifs x 2 during a crossfade~63 MB
beds    6 up at once x 60 s           ~121 MB
                                      ---------
total                                 ~184 MB stereo
                                      ~92 MB mono
```

**Mono halves it.** Ambience beds and single-instrument layers rarely need stereo; keep it for pads, strings and anything meant to sit wide. That one choice is the difference between a comfortable footprint and a heavy one.

Above that floor the console keeps whatever else it has already decoded, so a motif coming round again usually costs nothing, and evicts least-recently-used as it approaches `maxDecodedBytes` (default 320 MB). Audio that is currently sounding is never evicted, so the floor above is a true floor. Neither figure grows with how long the session runs. Lower the ceiling for tablets; the cost is a re-fetch when a motif returns, which has the queue lead (10 s) to complete in.

## Format

| | |
|---|---|
| Container | **Ogg Vorbis** (`.ogg`). See the note on MP3 below. |
| Sample rate | 48 kHz, or 44.1 kHz — one or the other throughout. |
| Channels | Stereo for wide beds and full layers; **mono halves the memory** and suits single instruments. |
| Music level | Mix each intensity level to about −18 LUFS, matched across levels so a crossfade does not jump. |
| Bed level | Normalise each bed to about −20 LUFS. The console applies −18/−12/−6 dB on top. |
| Bed length | 30–90 s, and give beds in one scene different lengths so they do not lock into a pattern. |

Motifs are chained by scheduling the next one to start the sample after the last one ends, so **every intensity level of a motif must be exactly the same length** and must not carry silence at either end. Ring-outs that cross the join should be printed into the head of the next motif, or left to the reverb tail of the stem itself.

**Avoid MP3.** The encoder pads both ends, and the padding survives decoding: motifs would no longer butt up cleanly and the layers of one motif would not line up. Ogg Vorbis, Opus and WAV do not. If you need a Safari fallback, serve `.m4a` from `resolveSrc` by feature test.

## Producing this in order

1. **One exploration motif per scene, all layers** (6 motifs, ~24 files). Every scene plays, and intensity works. This is the smallest thing worth demoing.
2. **Scene beds** (36 files, some shared). Most of the atmosphere lives here, and beds are far quicker to produce than scored motifs.
3. **The rest of each exploration pool** — the music stops feeling like a loop.
4. **Combat pools** — the combat toggle starts working.
5. **The rest of the bed library**, for the search.

Until a file exists, keep it out of the resolver so the console stays quiet about it: `assetLayout({ base, ext, available: urlsYouHaveUploaded })` returns `null` for anything not in the set, and `missingAssets(config, uploaded)` lists what is still outstanding.

### Levers, if this is too much

Unique music scales with **motifs × scenes**, and file count with **× layers**. Today: 6 scenes × 13 motifs × ~5 intensity levels. Halving the pool to four exploration and two combat motifs per scene halves both, at the cost of the order coming round twice as fast. Dropping a scene removes its whole column. Cutting a layer removes one file per motif and one step from the intensity control.
